subject: Edge tenant interaction threat scenarios and control rationale
messages:
From: Alex Monroe <alex.monroe@clearwaterbank.com>
To: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
Cc: security@clearwaterbank.com
Date: Tue, 20 Jul 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Request: edge tenant interaction threat scenarios and network diagram

Vanessa / Redwood team,

Thanks for the RFI packet so far. Clearwater's security review narrowed to a few remaining items we need to close our procurement checklist before SOW sign: a clear depiction of how tenants interact at the edge (both allowed and blocked flows), the likely attacker-led and failure-led threat scenarios between tenants, and the exact controls you apply to prevent cross-tenant data leakage (including KV cache behavior, sidecar models, and egress paths).

Specifically: 
- One annotated network diagram showing tenant edge, sidecar/proxy, control plane, and outbound egress paths.
- 3–4 short threat scenarios (attacker exploit, misconfiguration, compromised customer workload) that could lead to cross-tenant leakage and how each is mitigated.
- Evidence of KV cache isolation and encryption in practice (we may request a short design doc or spec).

Can you send these as a single packet and flag any open risks we should accept/manage? We have a security review window next week.

Thanks,
Alex Monroe
Senior InfoSec Manager
Clearwater Bank
security@clearwaterbank.com

From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Monroe <alex.monroe@clearwaterbank.com>
Cc: irene_choi@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 21 Jul 2027 11:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Request: edge tenant interaction threat scenarios and network diagram

Alex — thanks for the clear list. Attaching an overview packet and an annotated diagram to start (see attachment stubs below). Irene (security) and Marissa (solutions) are looped for technical detail and mitigation mapping.

What we've attached: 
- redwood_edge_interaction_overview.pdf — short narrative + summary table mapping controls to threat scenarios.
- redwood_network_edge_diagram_v2.png — annotated diagram showing tenant traffic lanes, sidecar placement, control plane demarcation, and egress choke points.

Quick highlights here: 
- Tenant compute lives in per-tenant logical compartments; traffic enters through a tenant-specific ingress path and is routed into a tenant-dedicated runtime slice. Sidecar proxies enforce per-request RBAC and TLS termination.
- KV caches are per-tenant by default and layered with encryption-at-rest and envelope encryption for cache hot keys. Cross-tenant cache references are blocked at the routing layer; additional application-level tokens validate provenance.
- Egress is tightly controlled via per-tenant allowlists and centralized egress gateways with explicit outbound ACLs; failures trigger fallback to a restricted model variant (no external calls).

Next steps: Irene will follow up with the control matrix and a short threat-model write-up that maps attacker paths to mitigations. If helpful we can do a 30-minute walkthrough next Tue/Wed.

Attachments: [redwood_edge_interaction_overview.pdf (application/pdf)], [redwood_network_edge_diagram_v2.png (image/png)]

Best,

From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Monroe <alex.monroe@clearwaterbank.com>, vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Thu, 22 Jul 2027 14:18:00 -0700
Subject: Control matrix and threat-model summary — tenant edge interactions

Alex / team — adding the technical detail requested below. I've included a short control matrix (attachment) and a concise threat-model summary here in the body for quick consumption. More artifacts (logs retention proof, SOC2 link) are attached via the Drive link Vanessa listed.

Isolation model (short):
- Logical tenancy: Each tenant is assigned an isolated runtime slice (namespaces + cgroups equivalent) with strict network namespaces. No direct layer-2 adjacency between tenant slices.
- Sidecar enforcement: Every workload is paired with a privileged sidecar process that performs mTLS termination, request-level auth (JWT provenance), and egress policy enforcement. Sidecars run with the minimum necessary capabilities and are constrained by kernel namespaces.
- Routing & control plane: Smart routing layer maps tokens to tenant slices and enforces per-tenant route tables; control plane signals (deploys, KV operations) are authenticated with customer-scoped identities.

KV cache specifics (threat-focused):
- Architecture: KV caches are sharded per-tenant. A tenant's cache shard lives on nodes that are logically isolated by namespace and access control lists; we do not co-locate untrusted tenant shards with highly privileged control plane caches.
- Encryption: Data at rest uses AES-256 with per-tenant keys; envelope keys are stored in a KMS-backed key hierarchy per customer. Keys are rotated on a schedule; rotation process is logged and auditable.
- Access: Cache access requires both (i) a signed request token validated by the sidecar, and (ii) tenant-scoped ACL enforced by the node-local cache daemon. This two-step check prevents token replay or lateral cache reads across tenants.

Representative threat scenarios and mitigations (3):
1) Compromised customer workload attempts to read another tenant's cached keys by calling shared cache API.
   - Attack vector: forged request token or lateral RPC to cache daemon.
   - Controls: sidecar token validation, node-local ACLs that check tenant id, per-tenant key encryption, and strict auditing of cache RPCs. Any anomaly triggers tenant quarantine and alert to SOC.

2) Misconfiguration leads to permissive egress rules, allowing exfiltration to external attacker-controlled endpoints.
   - Attack vector: overly broad allowlist on egress gateway OR misapplied routing policy during rollout.
   - Controls: immutable egress baseline for new tenants, policy rollouts via canary with automated drift detection, and egress gateway stub forcing outbound allowlist checks; emergency rollback policy reverts to restricted model variant.

3) Supply-chain compromise that affects a kernel-level component enabling lateral movement.
   - Attack vector: crafted payload that escalates to host and attempts to pivot to other tenant slices.
   - Controls: minimal host attack surface, signed and reproducible host images, runtime attestation (integrity checks on boot), and network micro-segmentation limiting pivot opportunities. Also periodic chaos testing of host hardening rules.

Evidence & telemetry:
- Flow logs and node-local audit traces retained for 365 days (configurable for enterprise customers).
- SOC2 Type II evidence available on request (link in Vanessa's Drive).
- Control matrix attached: isolation_control_matrix.xlsx maps each mitigation to the residual risk and compensating controls.

Open risks / residuals: 
- Very advanced, host-targeted zero-day exploits remain residual risk; mitigations reduce likelihood and detection time but cannot be proven to zero. We recommend Clearwater purchase the Enhanced Incident Response add-on for additional tabletop exercises and prioritized forensic access.

I'll follow up with a small KV cache spec that shows RPC auth flows if that helps. Happy to join a walkthrough.

Regards,
Irene Choi
Head of Security Engineering
Redwood Inference
irene_choi@redwood.ai

From: Alex Monroe <alex.monroe@clearwaterbank.com>
To: irene_choi@redwood.ai, vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 26 Jul 2027 08:25:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Control matrix and threat-model summary — tenant edge interactions

Irene — thanks, this is useful. A couple clarifying items before we close: 

1) KV cache access: your note says "two-step check" (signed token + node-local ACL). Can you confirm whether node-local ACLs are implemented as kernel-level permissions or an application-layer ACL? If application-layer, what's the hardening to prevent a compromised node-local process from returning arbitrary key values?

2) Cache deduplication / eviction: if tenant A and tenant B hash to the same cache slot (due to some shared dedup layer) could there be leakage via stale entries? Do you perform cache key scoping at the hashing layer or only at access time?

3) Finally, for the egress fallback: in the event of an egress gateway compromise, does the restricted model entirely disable external network calls, or does it allow only a short, audited path to an allowed telemetry endpoint? We need to understand what a fail-closed posture looks like operationally.

If you can provide a one-page answer addressing those three bullets we can route it to our architects and close the security review.

Best,
Alex

From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Monroe <alex.monroe@clearwaterbank.com>, vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 28 Jul 2027 16:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Control matrix and threat-model summary — tenant edge interactions (clarifications)

Alex — answers inline below, and attaching a short spec for the KV auth/encryption flows (kv_cache_encryption_spec.pdf).

1) Node-local ACLs: application-layer with kernel-enforced separation.
   - Implementation: the cache daemon enforces a strict application-layer ACL keyed by tenant id; the daemon itself runs in a dedicated namespace with limited capabilities. The node OS enforces file and socket ACLs so that only the cache daemon user can bind the cache socket. If the node-local process is compromised, kernel namespaces and seccomp filters limit what code can do; but because application-layer ACLs are relied upon, we add an additional cryptographic binding: each cache entry is encrypted with the tenant's envelope key so even a rogue process reading raw storage cannot decrypt values.

2) Deduplication / hashing: cache key scoping occurs at the hashing layer.
   - We namespace keys with tenant ids before any hashing/deduplication. Dedup layers operate on the fully-qualified key (tenantId:key); collisions become tenant-scoped and the server rejects requests that do not include the tenant provenance token. We also maintain per-tenant cache segments to prevent shared-slot re-use in the event of mis-hash collisions.

3) Egress fallback behavior: fail-closed but with narrowly permitted telemetry channels.
   - Operational posture: when an egress gateway is suspected/compromised, automated policy flips tenants into a restricted model variant that disables arbitrary external calls. By default, outbound is blocked except for a preconfigured, audited telemetry endpoint used for incident telemetry and health pings; access to that endpoint is authenticated and rate-limited. Customers can opt to disable telemetry in the restricted state for maximum isolation. All fallback events are logged and create an automatic incident ticket for both parties.

Residual notes: the extra encryption on cache entries is intentionally layered to protect against a node-local process compromise; combined with immutable host images, kernel filters, and per-tenant segments this reduces the practical risk of cross-tenant leakage to low.

Attachments referenced: [kv_cache_encryption_spec.pdf (application/pdf)]

If you'd like, we can prepare a short Appendix that extracts just these three answers for your architecture team to append to the procurement packet.

Regards,
Irene Choi
Head of Security Engineering
Redwood Inference
irene_choi@redwood.ai
